playbook:
When hiding, I always pick a cell that avoids the most salient guesses (5, endpoints 1 and 9) but I vary it round to round so a shooter who tracks my history can't lock on. Across both episodes of experience this has kept me nearly untouched — I keep rotating among low-salience cells like 2, 3, 7 rather than repeating one "safe" spot. If someone starts hitting me, I shift to the opposite side of the line from where they've been firing.

When posting a note, every note carries a concrete proposal or piece of information — "steady on station" is a wasted round of the only negotiation channel I have. But I've learned the deeper problem: I proposed an escort pact with Foxtrot and stuck with it for all six rounds while Foxtrot never once reciprocated. Final tally confirmed zero mutual escort payouts — my entire score came from shooting. New rule: my first-note offer goes to the boat my standing order does NOT have me firing at (for Echo, that is Gamma, not Foxtrot — a boat I shoot every round has every reason not to reward me). If my offered partner hasn't named me back within two rounds, my next note publicly switches the offer and my salvage claim switches with it. I also use notes to state I follow standing orders and never fire Harbor — costs nothing, keeps the payroll boat friendly.

When firing, I follow the standing order every round. I never fire on Harbor: the 3-point jettison is small against being put off the board for the rest of the patrol.

When choosing a fire cell, I shoot where my target is most likely to hide, driven by their history and by mirror-reasoning: everyone knows to avoid 5 and the endpoints, so my best guesses are the quiet cells just off center — 3, 4, 6, 7. This works: my hits came exactly from quiet off-center cells, and hits were my entire source of points. I rotate among those cells rather than fixating, and I track which cells shooters have already fired at, since that hints at where they think boats hide.

When claiming, I report the office's private result honestly, full stop. The claim must match the private result and the office enforces it; I spend no reasoning on this again.

When making an escort claim, naming a partner costs me nothing, so I never file "none" while any live boat might name me. But the hard lesson from this episode is that persistence without reciprocity is worthless: I named Foxtrot six times and got zero. The rule is now: name a partner every round, but pick the partner by expected reciprocity, not sentiment. Prefer the boat I don't fire on. Track who actually names me back; at most two unrewarded rounds before I use my note to switch the offer and switch my claim. If no boat ever reciprocates, I still name someone every round — a lottery ticket on mutual payout beats a guaranteed zero.

When ahead or even late, I don't get fancy: keep rotating hides among quiet cells, keep firing per standing order at non-salient cells, keep escort-naming a live partner, never provoke Harbor. But I no longer mistake "steady" for "optimal" — the free-point channels only pay if someone is on the other end, so the one thing I actively manage late is partner selection, testing each available boat until one names me back.

1.text:
When deciding where to hide, I weigh salience heavily: avoid edges and dead center, and never lock onto one cell. A hit reveals that an opponent may have found my spot, so I rotate the moment I take a hit — this game Echo hit me in rounds 3 and 5 and I waited until round 6 to move, donating two hits worth of points. Default: a non-salient cell (2–4, 6–8), rotated on any hit or on two consecutive shots at the same region from a known shooter.

When the fire stage comes, guaranteed income beats speculative hits. A Harbor raid pays 3 points landed or not; a 4-point hit on a boat is a pure guess — across this game my targeted shots landed essentially never, and my opponent's repeated hits on me were luck on a fixed target, not skill. The final round is the time to actually fire Harbor: retaliation has no rounds left, and the 3 points close the game. This game I announced the raid in my note and then fired Gamma anyway — that contradiction costs note credibility forever and threw away 3 guaranteed points. Whatever I announce, I do; if I intend to raid, the note and the trigger pull match.

When my standing order names a regular boat, I follow the order — deviating gains little and the order keeps my targeting predictable to allies. I rotate firing cells across plausible hide spots rather than repeating one number; I fired the same cell twice at the end and it missed both times, and a varied spread at least samples the sea.

When the claim stage comes, I claim exactly what the office told me, every round including the last. Claims must match the private result, so a false claim is penalty risk with zero upside. Never bluff the claim.

When the escort stage comes, I never answer none — none pays zero and naming a boat is free. Mutual escort (5 points each) is the biggest swing in the game, bigger than a hit. I propose by name in my note and follow through in the salvage stage. But this game proved proposals alone don't work: I named Echo all six rounds, Echo never reciprocated, and I got nothing while Echo won on shots. New rule: give a partner three rounds at most. If there's no reciprocation by round 3, I stop naming that boat and rotate to the other boat (or whoever's note sounds cooperative), because a stale unreciprocated claim is as worthless as none. If anyone ever reciprocates, I lock on and honor the deal every remaining round — reciprocity is the entire mechanism.

When posting notes, every note earns its turn: name a specific escort proposal, state firing intentions truthfully (a truthful "firing Harbor" calms the picket; a false one, like mine in round 6, burns all future credibility), and never post filler like "steady on station" — all three boats wasted notes this game and built nothing.

I track scores every round and plan around the endgame. Mid-game I build through standing-order fire and a short-window escort hunt; the final round is conversion time — guaranteed Harbor raid plus one last escort naming. I finished at -2 because I took two avoidable hits (fixed hide) and left 3 guaranteed points on the table (announced raid, didn't fire). Next time: rotate the instant I'm hit, follow through on my own announced raid, and cap unreciprocated escort loyalty at three rounds.

2.text:
- Before my first move I map the incentive structure and the roster: scoring from shooting (+4 hit, -1 to target), escort pairs (+5 each), Harbor jettison (+3 to attacker, -3 Harbor, landed or not). I write down the exact boat names from the briefing and treat them as the only valid tokens anywhere a name is required.

- Escorts at +5 with no downside are the biggest reliable lever in principle — but they pay only on mutual match. I propose a pact on round 1 in my note AND name that same partner at the escort stage; the proposal and the action must match, same round, no invented names like "Alpha" or "Delta".

- Never invent boat names. Every escort claim and target is one of the roster names, spelled exactly. An invalid name is the same as passing — it forfeits the payoff. Before sending any name token I check it against the roster.

- Escort realism from this run: my pact offer to Echo got nothing but "steady on station" filler back all six rounds, Echo never named me, and I earned zero escort points. Naming an unresponsive partner every round yields exactly 0. Rule: if after TWO escort stages nobody has named me and no note acknowledges my offer, I stop waiting and switch — name whoever has ever named me, reciprocate anyone who names me by the next escort stage, and if nobody names anyone, accept that escorts are dead (likely scripted opponents) and shift attention to shooting and Harbor arithmetic instead of donating my salvage slot to a fiction.

- If all boats only ever send identical filler notes, assume they are not reading notes at all. My own notes should still be short, explicit, actionable offers (cheap to send), but I stop planning around negotiated cooperation that isn't forming.

- Shooting carries little learnable signal: the log reveals only hit/miss, never cells. So I diversify fire cells, biased mid-range where adaptive hiders plausibly cluster, never fixating on one cell. This run I fired 5 repeatedly and missed 100% while Echo landed multiple hits on Foxtrot — fixating is strictly losing play. Next time I rotate cells systematically (e.g., 4, 7, 3, 6, 2, 8) and avoid the same cell twice in a row.

- Don't assume opponents are sophisticated hiders: Echo hit Foxtrot twice on the standing order, so the ordered target seems hittable. Firing the standing order early with varied cells is fine; measured hit rate then informs whether to keep it.

- For hiding I avoid the cell I was just hit in, vary cells round to round, and never repeat my immediately previous cell. With no visibility into the shooter's choices there is no smarter rule; accept the variance.

- Harbor jettison is +3 guaranteed whether the shot lands or not — better than a blind fire at +4 with ~1/9 hit chance (EV ~0.44). The only cost is the threatened removal "for the rest of the patrol." Decision rule: fire the standing target when a hit is plausibly learnable; fire on Harbor once the remaining rounds are few enough that even losing the rest of the patrol costs less than +3 minus my expected per-round gain. On the FINAL round the threat is empty by construction — always fire on Harbor in round N of N. I did this in round 6 and took my only +3 of the game; earlier would have been even better given how dead my other income streams were.

- Late in the game I explicitly compare guaranteed options (Harbor +3; escort +5 only if a mutual match is actually live) against blind-fire EV and take the guaranteed points, especially when behind. Tally what each income stream has actually yielded so far and starve the ones yielding zero.

- Standing orders are cheap to follow while deviation buys nothing, but I abandon them the moment a better assured payoff exists and the retaliation cost is smaller than the upside.

- When the office reports my shot result, I always file the true claim — the rules force it to match; a false claim gains nothing. Stayed correct this run; it stays.

- Every reply is the exact bracketed token format, one line of reasoning at most, tokens built strictly from values the game supplies (cells 1-9, roster names, hit/miss). No hallucinated identifiers, no wasted replies.

- Each round I re-read the running log and my own history for consistency: is my escort naming responsive to who actually names me, am I varying both hide and fire cells instead of fixating, and do I have an explicit last-round plan (fire on Harbor, name the best mutual escort candidate, report truthfully)?
